headline_marked: [[Lenovo: 'RAMageddon' is the new normal]] for memory prices, won't return to 2025 lows
headline: Lenovo: 'RAMageddon' is the new normal for memory prices, won't return to 2025 lows
summary: Lenovo predicts memory prices will remain elevated due to surging AI demand, even with new manufacturing capacity. The company outlined a 'RAMaggeddon Survival Guide' at ISC 2026, indicating a fundamental shift in industry economics.
details: Lenovo has declared that the ongoing 'RAMageddon' — the memory and storage shortage affecting nearly every tech market — is the new normal. At the International Supercomputing Conference (ISC) 2026, an executive reportedly stated that memory prices "will never be like it was last year," even presenting a "5 Step RAMaggeddon Survival Guide."

This statement implies that the unusually low memory prices seen in early 2025 are unlikely to return soon. Lenovo, the world's #1 PC OEM, anticipates continued growth in AI demand will keep prices for RAM, flash memory, and other components elevated for a prolonged period.

The company's broader message is that the economics of the memory industry have fundamentally changed. Lenovo argues that even as significant new manufacturing capacity comes online around 2028, demand from AI infrastructure is expected to absorb much of this additional output.

This absorption will prevent DRAM and NAND prices from returning to the lows observed over the past two years. SK hynix's plans to triple memory production capacity by 2034 support this view, as profit-hungry manufacturers are unlikely to invest heavily if they expected a return to oversupply.

Memory capacity itself is also becoming a critical consideration in server design. New dual-socket servers arriving next year will feature 16 memory channels per processor, meaning even modest configurations can require around 1 TB of installed memory to fully utilize available bandwidth.

Lenovo is not alone in predicting a prolonged memory crunch. Micron expects supply constraints through at least 2027, with gradual improvement beginning in 2028. SK hynix warns the shortage could persist until around 2030, as AI infrastructure continues to absorb wafer capacity.

These forecasts are backed by multi-year supply agreements worth approximately $100 billion that Micron has already signed with customers, underscoring how seriously hyperscalers are treating long-term memory availability. Even Apple has reportedly sought permission to source DRAM from a Pentagon-blacklisted Chinese memory maker, CXMT, highlighting the extreme value of additional supply.

Ironically, the shortage has made HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) more economically attractive relative to conventional system memory. DRAM manufacturers have redirected significant production capacity to higher-margin HBM for AI accelerators, reducing the supply of commodity DDR5 and LPDDR5 while demand for both remains high.
caption:

headline_marked: [[Austria lobbies EU]] to host Anthropic after US access curbs
headline: Austria lobbies EU to host Anthropic after US access curbs
summary: Austria is actively seeking to attract AI startup Anthropic to the EU, following recent US restrictions on the company's access to certain technologies. This move highlights growing European interest in becoming a hub for leading AI development.
details: Austria is making a significant push to convince the European Union to host Anthropic, a prominent AI startup. This diplomatic effort comes in the wake of new US restrictions that have impacted the company's access to crucial technologies.

The US government has recently implemented measures limiting certain AI companies' access to advanced computing resources and data, prompting some firms to explore international alternatives. Anthropic, known for its Claude large language models, is a key player in the AI landscape.

Austria's lobbying highlights a broader European ambition to cultivate its own AI ecosystem and reduce reliance on US-centric tech infrastructure. Attracting a company like Anthropic could significantly bolster the EU's position in global AI development.

Hosting Anthropic could bring substantial economic and technological benefits to the chosen EU member state, including job creation, investment in research, and the development of cutting-edge AI applications within European regulatory frameworks.

The move also signals a growing geopolitical competition for AI talent and resources. European nations are increasingly looking to position themselves as attractive destinations for AI innovation, offering different regulatory environments and market access compared to the US.
